title: The quantization quality tradeoff: empirical state in 2025
summary: Where INT4, INT8, and FP8 quantization stand today on frontier-class models. INT8 weights are essentially free quality-wise; INT4 with AWQ is production-acceptable for most use cases; FP8 hardware (H100) opens new options. Where each quantization method's quality cost actually lands.
abstract: Quantization is now table stakes for production LLM serving. Memory savings of 2-4× from fp16 down to int4 are routine; the question is at what quality cost. This paper reviews the 2024-2025 empirical state across the dominant methods (GPTQ, AWQ, QLoRA, SmoothQuant) on standard evaluation suites, and identifies where the quality cost is concentrated. The honest summary: int8 weights are nearly free; int4 with AWQ loses 1-3% on standard benchmarks but more on long-tail capabilities; FP8 on H100s offers a middle ground with hardware-specific advantages. Production deployments should measure on their actual eval, not on the headline benchmarks.
contentIntro:
## What we're measuring

Quantization saves memory. By how much, and at what quality cost? The answer matters for every production LLM deployment in 2024-2025.

This paper covers:

- The dominant quantization methods (GPTQ, AWQ, SmoothQuant, QLoRA, FP8)
- Their reported quality costs on standard benchmarks
- Where headline numbers diverge from actual production behavior
- Recommendations for picking a quantization scheme

[[quantization]]
contentUndergrad:
## The methods

**INT8 weight-only**. Quantize weights to 8-bit integers; keep activations in fp16/bf16. Negligible quality cost (typically < 0.5% on standard benchmarks). 2× memory savings vs fp16. Default for most production deployments.

**INT4 with GPTQ** (Frantar et al. 2022). Layer-wise optimization minimizing reconstruction error. ~1-3% quality cost on most benchmarks. 4× memory savings.

**INT4 with AWQ** (Lin et al. 2023). Activation-aware scaling. Empirically beats GPTQ. Now the default for int4 in most serving stacks. ~0.5-2% quality cost on most benchmarks.

**INT4 with QuIP/QuIP#** (Chee et al. 2024). Adds incoherence preprocessing for better int4 (and even int2) quality. Cutting edge; not yet widely deployed.

**FP8** (E4M3/E5M2). 8-bit floating point. Available natively on H100 and newer hardware. Different from int8 in that it preserves more dynamic range. Quality typically between fp16 and int8.

**SmoothQuant** (Xiao et al. 2023). Migrates quantization difficulty between weights and activations to make int8 activations viable. Enables full int8 (not just weight-only) at modest quality cost.

**QLoRA** (Dettmers et al. 2023). For fine-tuning: load base in int4 (NF4), train LoRA in fp16. Reduces fine-tune memory 4× without retraining the base.

## Quality costs by benchmark

Aggregating reported numbers across LLaMA-2 7B, LLaMA-2 70B, and Mistral 7B, on common benchmarks:

| Method | MMLU | HumanEval | GSM8K | MT-Bench |
|--------|------|-----------|-------|----------|
| fp16 (baseline) | reference | reference | reference | reference |
| int8 weights | -0.0 to -0.3 | ~equal | ~equal | ~equal |
| int4 GPTQ | -1 to -2 | -1 to -3 | -1 to -2 | -0.1 to -0.3 |
| int4 AWQ | -0.3 to -1.5 | -0.5 to -2 | -0.5 to -1.5 | -0.05 to -0.2 |
| int4 QuIP# | comparable to AWQ | comparable | comparable | comparable |

The headline: at int8, quality is essentially free. At int4 with AWQ, the cost is small enough to be production-acceptable. AWQ has consistently outperformed GPTQ.

## Where headline numbers mislead

The averages above hide the failure modes. Quantization quality cost is not uniformly distributed across tasks:

- **Long-tail tasks degrade more.** Rare-token-heavy tasks (low-resource languages, esoteric coding tasks, specific domains) lose more than the headline. Some teams report 5-15% degradation at int4 on long-tail tasks where MMLU only loses 1-2%.

- **Long context degrades more.** Quantized KV-cache amplifies errors. Generation quality at 32K context can degrade noticeably even when 4K is fine.

- **Specific behaviors break first.** Refusal behavior, format-following, JSON output — small but observable degradations show up in production before benchmarks pick them up.

For production deployments: don't trust the headline numbers. Run your own eval on your actual traffic patterns before committing to a quantization recipe.
contentGrad:
## Hardware considerations

Quantization isn't purely a software story. The right precision depends on what your hardware accelerates:

- **A100 (Ampere)**: int8 tensor cores. fp16 + bf16. No native int4; int4 quantization gives memory savings but not compute savings on this hardware.

- **H100 (Hopper)**: adds FP8 (E4M3 + E5M2) tensor cores. int8 still supported. NVIDIA's TransformerEngine library uses FP8 for both weights and activations during inference. ~2× throughput vs fp16 on H100 for FP8 matmuls.

- **Consumer GPUs (RTX 4090, etc.)**: int4 with AWQ is the practical sweet spot. Memory is the binding constraint; int4 fits a 70B model in 24GB while int8 doesn't.

- **Apple Silicon**: 4-bit GGUF quantization via llama.cpp. Different recipe (k-quants, i-quants); similar empirical quality to AWQ.

## QLoRA in detail

For fine-tuning, QLoRA has become the practical default at memory-constrained scales. The key trick: int4 NF4 (Normal Float 4) quantization, designed to match the distribution of normally-distributed weights.

The NF4 binning isn't uniform — it's spaced to match the quantiles of a normal distribution. Empirically, this preserves more of the weight matrix's information than uniform int4 quantization. Combined with double quantization (quantize the quantization constants themselves) and paged optimizers, QLoRA fits a 70B fine-tune on a single 48GB GPU.

The quality story: QLoRA fine-tunes are nearly indistinguishable from fp16 LoRA fine-tunes on standard evaluations. The base model's int4 quantization is a small quality hit; the LoRA adapter is fp16 and recovers most of it.

## What to use, when

A practical decision tree:

- **Single GPU, 7B-13B model, plenty of memory**: fp16 or int8. Use AWQ if you want the speed.
- **Single GPU, 70B+ model, memory-constrained**: int4 with AWQ. Validate on your eval set.
- **H100 cluster, latency-sensitive**: FP8 with TransformerEngine. Hardware-native.
- **Fine-tuning a 70B base on a single GPU**: QLoRA. NF4 + LoRA fp16.
- **Edge deployment, <10GB memory budget**: int4 GGUF (llama.cpp) or QuIP# if you can train.

For any choice: benchmark on your actual production task. Headline numbers are reported on MMLU; your customers don't query MMLU.

## Where the field is going

Active research is on int2 and ternary quantization. **BitNet** (Microsoft 2024) trains models from scratch with 1-bit weights and shows competitive quality at the small-model regime. **The Era of 1-bit LLMs** (Ma et al. 2024) extends to 1.58-bit (ternary -1/0/+1) with similar conclusions.

If 1-bit / ternary quantization becomes viable at frontier scale, the deployment economics change dramatically. A 70B model at 1-bit is 8.75 GB — fits on a single consumer GPU. The hardware would need updating (current GPUs don't have native 1-bit tensor cores), but the demand would justify it.
